findings.where: First screen, the row of five outlined capsules under the lead (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation), at desktop and phone
findings.fault: The capsules each draw their own white outline in the link colour and sit just above the email button. They look like filter chips or links to topic pages, but none of them does anything (the parts map lists them as static). Topic chips are the pattern a bank official expects to filter articles by, so they will try one. Nothing happens, and the page seems broken just before the main action.
findings.who_objects: The bank official, who clicks 'PPP Law' to find Mark's writing on PPP law and gets no response. The house's function walk also objects: a static fact has borrowed the selectable chip's shape.

findings.where: First screen, the white email button 'Mark.Moseley@MMMinfra.com →'
findings.fault: According to the parts map, the page's one action links to '#' rather than to a mailto with the address. Clicking it does nothing: no mail window opens and the page does not move. The arrow promises to take the visitor somewhere.
findings.who_objects: The official who has decided to write and clicks the obvious button, then has to copy the address by hand. The founder also objects, because the first screen is meant to be the homepage exactly as a visitor sees it.

findings.where: First screen, the blue field: the diagonal stripe pattern across the whole hero, and the large ghost letters 'PPP' behind the heading
findings.fault: The field is not the flat colour the page itself describes. The tile's own Texture panel says 'No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient', yet the hero is covered in diagonal hatching. A pale oversized 'PPP' also sits behind 'In my view'. Both add busyness directly under the heading and lead, and the ghost letters read like a consultancy's label behind Mark's own words.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for care over 'how busy or quiet the ground is' and for a look no consultancy could own, and who will see a tile that contradicts its own specimen. The visitor also objects, because they read the heading and lead through stripes and a watermark.

findings.where: Article specimen, the PDF link 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' and the three list bullets
findings.fault: The article brings in an orange-red that appears nowhere else. The palette panel on the same page says 'Four colours and no accent', with links and the action in house blue. Here, the one link on the article page (to the PDF list the research calls the product) and the bullets are in an unnamed red. Links in the article now look different from links on the rest of the site.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for every tile to be built in the house blue and grey and will read the red as an off-brand accent. The visitor also objects, because blue means 'link' elsewhere on the site and red means it here.

findings.where: Article specimen, the image caption, the subhead 'So, what are the key 'chapter topics'?', the three-item list and the PDF row below it, at desktop and phone
findings.fault: The rhythm breaks where the brief said it must hold. The subhead sits almost on top of the image caption, with less space above it than below, so it reads as part of the photo's caption block. The list items are set solid, with far tighter line spacing than the 30 px body text, and on phone the wrapped items run together. The last item touches the hairline and PDF row beneath it.
findings.who_objects: The founder, because the brief asks this specimen to prove the type 'sits on a rhythm that holds when she adds an image, a caption, a list or a subhead'. Angélique, who will add exactly these elements. The reader of Mark's article, who has to work to find where the section starts and where each list item ends.

findings.where: Article specimen, the title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' against the subhead 'So, what are the key 'chapter topics'?', worst at phone
findings.fault: The subhead is as large as the article title on desktop. On phone it looks larger than the title, with the same heavy weight. The page has no clear top heading, and the section break competes with the article's name.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning the article, who cannot tell from size which line names the article and which names a section.

findings.where: Header lockup, top left of the first screen, at desktop and phone
findings.fault: Mark's name does not lead. The aqueduct mark comes first, and 'Mark M. Moseley' is set small beside it at nav-like size, so on first view the eye goes to the heading, then the photograph, and reaches the name last. The only large rendering of his name on the page is the small bold start of the photo caption.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose personal-advisor test requires that 'his name leads, with the logo beside it'. The official, who leaves the first screen remembering a sentence and a face but not whom to write to.

findings.where: Header lockup and Texture panel, the aqueduct mark reversed to white on the blue field
findings.fault: The mark is shown as a white reversed version that the brand sheet does not list as a version Mark holds. The page presents it as settled ('The mark reverses to white on it'), although a new logo version needs Mark's agreement.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo it is, and the founder, who would have to put the reversed version to Mark before the tile can lead.

findings.fault: On phone, the photograph and its placeholder caption fill the first screen. Mark's line starts low on that screen, and the lead, the topics and the email action are all pushed to the second screen. A visitor on a phone sees a face but not what he does, for whom, or how to reach him until they scroll.
findings.who_objects: The official opening the link from LinkedIn on a phone, who on the first screen cannot tell that this advisor works on PPP law for development banks and has no visible way to write.

findings.fault: The apostrophe in 'World's' renders as a straight tick, while the subhead below uses curly quotes ('chapter topics'). The mismatch shows on the largest line of the article.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, and Mark as a lawyer who drafts texts, who would notice the inconsistent marks in a display heading.

findings.where: Type pair panel, the 'Source Sans 3' sample beside 'In my view, Gelasio'
findings.fault: The sans sample floats lower than the serif sample, with no shared baseline or top. It looks misplaced rather than deliberately placed.
findings.who_objects: The founder, reviewing the specimen, for whom the pairing looks less finished than it is.
